compareCandidate.label: Exothermic vs. endothermic
compareCandidate.description: An exothermic reaction RELEASES energy — it heats its surroundings, like a burning fire or a hand warmer. An endothermic reaction ABSORBS energy — it cools its surroundings, like a cold pack or cooking an egg. One gives out, the other takes in.

parts: Energy leaves as heat and light
processes: Warming the surroundings as heat or light
plainLanguageExplanation: An exothermic reaction is a chemical reaction that releases energy to its surroundings. The name literally means 'heat going out' — exo (out) + therm (heat). When such a reaction happens, the chemicals give off energy, usually as heat and sometimes as light. Think of a burning fire: the wood and oxygen react, and the reaction pours out heat and light. A hand warmer is another example — you crack the pack, a chemical reaction starts, and it releases heat that warms your hands. Even your own body is a furnace of exothermic reactions: the food you eat reacts with oxygen, releasing the energy that keeps you warm and powers your muscles. Why does this happen? The reactants in an exothermic reaction hold MORE energy than the products that form. The extra energy has to go somewhere, so the reaction releases it into the surroundings — which is why the surroundings get warmer. Exothermic reactions power fires, engines, hand warmers, and life itself.

keyFacts.label: Examples
keyFacts.value: Fire, hand warmers, engines, your body's metabolism

whyItMatters: Exothermic reactions are the engine of everyday warmth and energy. Fire, engines, hand warmers, and the metabolism keeping your body at 37°C are all exothermic. Understanding them explains where heat comes from, why fires feel hot, and how energy moves between chemicals and the world.
didYouKnow: Your body runs on exothermic reactions — the food you eat reacts with oxygen and releases heat. That is why you stay warm at 37°C even in a cold room.
compareReason: The exothermic and endothermic reactions are opposite energy partners — comparing releasing with absorbing makes the whole energy story of reactions crystal clear.
